narrative:
The model estimates an 81% probability that you will leave your job, so you were denied a promotion because the organization sees you as a high retention risk. This is a forecast, not a verdict on your performance, but it means a promotion is currently judged unlikely to keep you.

The strongest influence was your overall work experience of one to five years. That range is common among employees predicted to stay—about half fall there—so this signal modestly pointed toward staying. However, it was outweighed by stronger leaving signals. The clearest push toward leaving came from your having other job opportunities: only about one in four employees predicted to stay reported outside opportunities, so your situation raises concern that you may already have alternatives. Your sector, “other,” also pushed toward leaving, as it is less common among stayers than medical or education and may reflect different retention patterns.

Before revisiting promotion, discuss what would make you stay: a concrete career path, development, recognition, fair pay, and job stability. Explore the outside opportunities you are considering and whether an internal role or clearer promotion timeline could address them. The 81% estimate should prompt a retention conversation, not be treated as a final verdict.
